TVA Brown's Ferry Nuclear Plant, Units 1, 2, and 3, under construction.

The large object that is the subject of the photo is the Mark I primary containment drywell ("inverted lightbulb") of Brown's Ferry Unit 1. Behind and to the left, you can see the top of Unit 2's drywell, and in the far background you can see the top of Unit 3's. Why do I like this image? In my opinion, it encompasses the American can-do attitude of the late 60's, early 70's. We just landed men on the fucking moon. We split the atom and made electricity. We're gonna save the world, and we're gonna do it bigly - so here we are, building three nuclear power plants at once.

Details on Unit 1, the big hole in the side is either for the personnel airlock, or for the equipment hatch. I'd wager the latter. All the stuff sticking out of the drywell are penetrations, used to bring pipes, instrument lines, or electrical cables in and out. Since they're an obvious weak point, they are built to be the strongest part of the containment. You can see multiple pipes kinda behind the lower drywell, pointing to the right. Those are for main steam and feedwater lines (the turbine buildings are under construction to the far right). Just above the sphere part of the drywell, you can see two penetrations going to the left (easier seen on Unit 2). Those are probably for Core Spray, one of the emergency systems used to cool the core.

Below the drywell and around it, you can see the Torus. Back in the 60's, when the current set of nuclear units was being designed, the worst possible scenario thought of was a Loss-of-Coolant-Accident, or LOCA. This involves some kind of leak of water (coolant) from the reactor. Since the water is at high temperature and pressure, it would immediately and violently flash into steam. All containments were build to withstand this kind of accident. Westinghouse built very, very large containments meant to absorb this energy and slowly cool it down (basically with air conditioners). General Electric said no, that's expensive. Instead, we know all this energy is in steam - so we will force the steam to go under water, where it will be quenched and take care of all this energy. So, the torus is about half full of water. The steam from the hypothetical coolant leak leaves the drywell through the very large pipes you see, and enters a ring inside of the torus. It's then vented under water.
